content:
One recurring critique says Muhammad (peace be upon him) does not meet the standard set by earlier prophets: no parted sea, no raised dead, nothing for a skeptic in Mecca to see. It adds that a specific prophecy in the Quran about the Byzantines failed, or at best reads as too vague to test, and offers a medical alternative to revelation itself, that the experience behind it was a seizure. Put together, the claim is that nothing about the man or the book required a prophetic explanation.

The fair form of the objection deserves a fair hearing. The Quran genuinely does decline to stage the kind of spectacle Moses or Jesus are remembered for, and a critic is entitled to ask why. Five entries below take the claim at its strongest: what the Quran itself says about signs, what the hadith record claims beyond the Quran, what the Byzantine prophecy actually says and how it reads against the history, where the epilepsy theory comes from, and what standard of evidence the objection is actually asking revelation to meet.

The Meccans did ask for spectacle, and the Quran records the list: make a spring gush from the ground, own a garden of palms and vines with rivers running through it, drop the sky on them in pieces, bring God and the angels before them, possess a house of gold, or climb into heaven and bring back a book they could read (17:90–93).[1] The reply is not a counter-miracle. It is a question put back to the objector: a man, a messenger, walking in the markets and eating food like everyone else, what else could he be sent as (17:94–95; 25:7)?[2]

Elsewhere the Quran states the policy outright. Those who do not expect to meet God ask for angels to descend or for God to be seen directly; they have grown arrogant (25:21).[3] The disbelievers swear their most earnest oaths that a sign would make them believe, and the reply is that signs are with God alone, and that a sign would not move them even if it came, because hearts already decided against belief are not short on evidence (6:109–110).[4] Asked directly for a sign, the answer given to Muhammad to speak is “signs are only with God, and I am only a plain warner”, followed by the question that does the work in this passage: “Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book, recited to them?” (29:50–51).[5] The book itself is offered as the sign, with a standing challenge attached: produce even one chapter like it (2:23; 10:38; 17:88).[6]

A critic can still find this unsatisfying, and that is a reasonable place to stop, short of theft or contradiction. What the objection cannot fairly say is that the absence of spectacle was concealed. The Quran puts the demand in the mouths of its opponents, states that it is refusing it, and gives its reason in the text available to anyone, which is a strange thing for a deception to do.

Because the Quran's own claim to a sign is the book, critics sometimes frame “no miracles” as settled by that fact alone. It is not quite that simple: later hadith literature, outside the Quran, does report specific events, and two are cited often enough to deserve a direct answer rather than a dismissal.

The first is the splitting of the moon. Surah al-Qamar opens, “The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split” (54:1).[7] Ibn Mas’ud reports that the moon split into two parts during the Prophet's lifetime, one half over a mountain, and that he told those present to bear witness (Bukhari 4864; also Tirmidhi 3285, graded sahih).[8] Anas adds that the people of Mecca had asked for a sign and were shown this (Bukhari 4867–4868).[9] Classical commentators, among them al-Tahawi and Ibn Kathir, treat the reports as mutawatir, meaning carried by enough independent lines that collusion on a fabrication is judged implausible by the standards of hadith criticism.[10] That is a verdict from inside the tradition, and a critic outside it is not bound to accept it. The honest difficulty for the believer is that no outside astronomical record of a split moon survives from the period, and the honest difficulty for the critic is that a momentary, regional event is not the kind of thing seventh-century observers elsewhere had the means to record either way. Some early reciters and commentators also read the verb as a statement about the Last Hour rather than a completed sign in the Prophet's lifetime, which shows the matter was not read as self-evident even by Muslims early on.[11]

The second is water reported to have flowed from between his fingers for companions to drink from, narrated by several of those present, including Jabir ibn Abdillah and Anas ibn Malik, at more than one occasion during military expeditions (Bukhari 3572, 3576).[12] As with the moon, this is a report carried by named companions and preserved by the same critical apparatus that preserves the Quran's legal and historical material, not a claim made by the Quran on its own authority. A reader is free to weigh hadith evidence differently than Quranic text, and many classical and modern scholars do exactly that. What should not stand is the claim that no miracle beyond the book was ever reported. One was; it simply was not reported by the book itself.

Surah al-Rum opens in the years after a real defeat. The Sassanid Persians had routed Byzantine forces and, by 614, taken Jerusalem; Meccan polytheists, who favoured Persia's cause over Christian Byzantium, took the news as a sign that their own position was the stronger one.[13] The Quran's response is a prediction: “The Byzantines have been defeated, in the nearest land, but they, after their defeat, will be victorious, within a few years” (30:2–4).[14] Muslim tradition reports that Abu Bakr staked a wager on the outcome with a Meccan opponent, a detail preserved in commentary on the verse though graded by some hadith critics as less firmly established than the verse's content itself.[15]

The history runs the way the verse says it would. Heraclius's counteroffensive, beginning in 622 and culminating in the destruction of the main Persian field army at Nineveh in 627, reversed the Byzantine collapse and led to the return of Jerusalem and the True Cross by 629–630.[16] “A few years”, bid’ sinin in the Arabic, is a flexible idiom that classical lexicographers place between three and nine, or in some readings up to ten.[17] The fair objection is exactly that flexibility: a window of three to roughly ten years, against a reversal that unfolded gradually across the 620s, is wide enough that a critic can reasonably call the prophecy difficult to falsify rather than sharply confirmed. A separate internal dispute exists over the verb's vowelling, since a minority reading, ghalabat rather than the standard ghulibat, would make the Byzantines the victors rather than the defeated party from the start; specialists in Quranic recitation judge this variant weakly transmitted against the standard text, which is the reading every surviving manuscript tradition and both the Meccan audience's reaction and the following verses assume.[18]

Taken on the standard text, the prophecy named the losing side correctly, named the general outcome correctly, and did so from Mecca, before the military situation had turned. A critic can still hold that the dating window is loose enough to be unimpressive as a test of foreknowledge. That is a defensible position. It is a narrower claim than “the prophecy failed”, which the recorded history does not support.

A modern-sounding diagnosis has an old paper trail. The historian of medicine Owsei Temkin traced the charge to Byzantine polemic, written by an empire at war with the early Muslim state and hostile to its founder on that basis before any medical question was asked; John of Damascus, writing in the eighth century, is among the earliest to frame Muhammad's experience in pathological terms.[19] The theory resurfaced among nineteenth- and early twentieth-century European biographers, including D. S. Margoliouth and William Muir, both of whom read the physical strain described in hadith reports as symptomatic of a seizure disorder.[20]

The site's companion piece on the first revelation covers this ground at length, including the Aisha report of sweat and strain that the theory leans on, and W. Montgomery Watt's direct reply: the symptoms described do not match epilepsy, which causes physical and mental decline, whereas the Prophet kept the full use of his faculties to the end of a public life that lasted over twenty years and produced coherent, memorised speech after every episode.[21] The Moroccan scholar Muhammad Benaboud, reviewing a century of this Orientalist literature, reached the same conclusion: the epilepsy charge is a medieval polemical theme that nineteenth- and twentieth-century scholarship kept recycling in modern dress, not a finding the clinical picture in the sources actually supports.[22] Readers who want the full treatment, including the demonic-possession version of the same charge, should see “6 answers to the claim the first revelation was demonic”; this entry exists to place the theory's history on the record rather than repeat that argument.

Underneath the specific charges sits a broader question: what would count? The Quran's own answer is that compelled belief was never the point. “Even if We sent down angels to them, and the dead spoke to them, and We gathered everything before them in ranks, they would not believe, unless God wills it” (6:111).[23] That is a claim about human beings generally, and the Bible supplies its own test case: a crowd that watched the plagues fall on Egypt built a golden calf within weeks of its deliverance (Exodus 32:1–4), and observers of Jesus's own reported healings in the Gospels are shown attributing them to demonic power rather than converting on the spot (Matthew 12:22–24).[24] Spectacle, on the record both traditions keep, has not reliably produced belief even when granted.

None of this proves the Quran is revelation; it was never meant to by itself. What it shows is that “no miracles like Moses or Jesus” is a difference in genre. The Quran states its reasons for that difference in the open, rather than hoping no one asks. The Byzantine prophecy named the losing side and the eventual outcome before the reversal happened, on a timeline loose enough to debate but not so loose as to be empty. And the clinical theory offered as a tidier explanation than revelation has a documented origin in a hostile empire's war propaganda, and has not survived contact with historians who examined it on the medical evidence rather than inherited it as settled.

The bottom line

The Quran withholds the showy sign and says so, pointing to itself and to a documented pattern of rejection that survived earlier miracles too. The hadith record does add two specific miracle reports beyond the book, carried by named witnesses rather than the Quran's own voice. The Byzantine prophecy named the right losers and the right eventual winners from Mecca, inside a wide but not unlimited window. The epilepsy theory traces to Byzantine polemic and has been rejected by historians, including skeptical ones, who checked it against the clinical record rather than the slogan.

A critic can still hold that none of this amounts to proof of prophethood, and that is a position the evidence leaves open to hold. “No evidence was offered” and “the prophecy simply failed” are narrower claims, and the sources, Muslim and otherwise, do not support either one.

  1. Quran 17:90–93.
  2. Quran 17:94–95; 25:7.
  3. Quran 25:21.
  4. Quran 6:109–110.
  5. Quran 29:50–51.
  6. Quran 2:23; 10:38; 17:88.
  7. Quran 54:1.
  8. Sahih al-Bukhari 4864 (Book of Commentary, chapter on Surah al-Qamar), report of Ibn Mas’ud, checked on sunnah.com; Jami al-Tirmidhi 3285, graded sahih, same report.
  9. Sahih al-Bukhari 4867–4868 (Book of Commentary, chapter on Surah al-Qamar), reports of Anas ibn Malik, checked on sunnah.com.
  10. Al-Tahawi, Mushkil al-Athar, and Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Qur'an al-'Azim, on Quran 54:1, both describing the transmission as mutawatir.
  11. Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Qur'an al-'Azim, on Quran 54:1, noting the reading of the verse as referring to a sign of the approaching Hour.
  12. Sahih al-Bukhari 3572 and 3576 (Book of the Merits of the Companions), reports of Jabir ibn Abdillah and Anas ibn Malik, checked on sunnah.com.
  13. Walter E. Kaegi, Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2003), on the Sassanid capture of Jerusalem in 614 and the Meccan reaction; Quran 30:2–4 and classical commentary on its occasion of revelation.
  14. Quran 30:2–4.
  15. Jami al-Tirmidhi, commentary tradition on Surah al-Rum, the report of a wager between Abu Bakr and a Meccan opponent over the prophecy's outcome.
  16. On Heraclius's campaign of 622–627 and the recovery of Jerusalem and the True Cross by 629–630, see Walter E. Kaegi, Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2003), chapters 5–6.
  17. Classical Arabic lexicons (e.g. Lane's Arabic-English Lexicon) on bid’ as a number between three and nine or ten; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, commentary on 30:4.
  18. On the ghalabat/ghulibat reading, see Faraz Rabbani, “Is the Variant Reading of Ghalabat al-Rum Soundly Transmitted?”, SeekersGuidance, assessing the chain for ghalabat as weak against Ibn al-Jazari's conditions for an accepted reading.
  19. Owsei Temkin, The Falling Sickness: A History of Epilepsy from the Greeks to the Beginnings of Modern Neurology (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1971), on the Byzantine origin of the epilepsy charge; John of Damascus, De Haeresibus, chapter 100, among the earliest polemical sources to frame the charge.
  20. D. S. Margoliouth, Mohammed and the Rise of Islam (New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1905); William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (London: Smith, Elder & Co., 1861).
  21. W. Montgomery Watt, Muhammad at Mecca (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1953), 57; see also the site piece “6 answers to the claim the first revelation was demonic.”
  22. Muhammad Benaboud, "Orientalism on the Revelation of the Prophet: The Cases of W. Montgomery Watt, Maxime Rodinson, and Duncan Black MacDonald," The American Journal of Islamic Social Sciences 3, no. 2 (1986): 309–310, identifying the epilepsy charge as a medieval theme (alongside "imposter" and "heretic") that recurs through nineteenth- and twentieth-century Orientalist scholarship on the Prophet.
  23. Quran 6:111.
  24. Exodus 32:1–4; Matthew 12:22–24.
